parts.text: Describe how data is stored on a magnetic hard disk drive.

parts.text: Explain what is meant by virtual memory.
parts.answer: Part of secondary storage (e.g. the hard disk or SSD) is used as if it were extra RAM when RAM is full.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how virtual memory is used when a student opens many large applications at once.
parts.answer: When RAM becomes full, data/pages that are not currently being used are moved from RAM to virtual memory on secondary storage, freeing RAM for the data needed now; when those pages are needed again they are swapped back into RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: RAM fills up; pages/data not currently in use are transferred to virtual memory (secondary storage); space in RAM is then used for the new data/application; pages are swapped back into RAM when needed.

2. Carries signals such as 'memory read' and 'memory write'.
3. Holds the address of the memory location that is about to be accessed.
4. Holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
parts.answer: 1 Memory data register (MDR); 2 Control bus; 3 Memory address register (MAR); 4 Current instruction register (CIR).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct name: MDR; control bus; MAR; CIR.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Refer to the registers and buses used.
parts.answer: The address in the PC is copied into the MAR; the address is sent along the address bus to memory; a read signal is sent on the control bus; the instruction at that address is sent along the data bus to the MDR; the instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR; the PC is incremented by 1.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: PC holds address of next instruction; address copied from PC to MAR; address sent via address bus; control unit sends read signal on control bus; instruction transferred via data bus; instruction stored in MDR; instruction copied to CIR; PC incremented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens in the decode stage.
parts.answer: The control unit decodes (interprets) the instruction in the CIR.
parts.working: B1 instruction in the CIR is decoded/interpreted by the control unit.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the address bus is unidirectional but the data bus is bidirectional.
parts.answer: Addresses only travel from the CPU to memory, whereas data must travel both from memory to the CPU (reading) and from the CPU to memory (writing).
parts.working: 1 mark: address bus carries addresses only from CPU (MAR) to memory. 1 mark: data bus carries data to and from the CPU (read and write).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the accumulator (ACC).
parts.answer: It temporarily stores the result of calculations carried out by the ALU.
parts.working: B1 holds intermediate/final results of ALU operations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: During one cycle the PC contains 52. State the value in the PC after the fetch stage has finished, assuming instructions are stored one per address and no jump occurs.
parts.working: B1 53 – the PC is incremented by 1 during the fetch stage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: CPU components and the fetch-decode-execute cycle

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An instruction is stored at memory address 200 and the next instruction is at address 201. The instruction at 200 tells the CPU to add the value stored at address 350 to the accumulator.
Describe, step by step, how the CPU fetches and executes this instruction, naming each register and bus involved.
parts.answer: Fetch: 200 is copied from PC to MAR; sent on address bus with a read signal on the control bus; instruction travels on data bus to MDR; copied to CIR; PC becomes 201. Decode: CU decodes the instruction in CIR. Execute: 350 is placed in the MAR; value at address 350 is read via the data bus into the MDR; the ALU adds the MDR value to the ACC; result is stored in the ACC.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: PC (200) → MAR; address bus used; read signal via control bus; instruction to MDR via data bus; MDR → CIR; PC incremented to 201; CU decodes instruction; operand address 350 → MAR; data at 350 loaded into MDR; ALU performs addition; result stored in ACC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the PC is incremented during the fetch stage instead of after the instruction has been executed.
parts.answer: So that it already holds the address of the next instruction, ready for the next cycle; if the instruction is a jump, the execute stage can then overwrite the PC with the new address.
parts.working: 1 mark: PC then points to the next instruction ready for the next fetch. 1 mark: a jump/branch instruction can replace the PC value during execute.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: The list of all the commands (machine code operations) that a particular CPU can process.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: The clock sends out regular pulses that synchronise all CPU operations; each step of the cycle happens in time with the clock pulses.

Byte 2: 0 0 1 1 0 1 1 0
Byte 3: 0 1 1 1 0 0 0 1
Byte 4: 1 0 0 0 1 1 1 1
Byte 5: 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 0
Byte 6: 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 1
Parity byte: 1 1 0 1 1 1 1 0

parts.answer: It is not known whether the error happened on the way to the receiver or on the way back; it doubles the amount of data transmitted.
parts.working: B1 cannot tell in which direction the error occurred / doubles transmission time or traffic.

A cricket academy in Sialkot records the runs scored by its 20 players in each of 10 matches. The program uses:

• a two-dimensional array Runs[1:20, 1:10] of type INTEGER

• calculate each player's total and average runs (average rounded to 1 decimal place) and output the name, total and average
• find and output the name of the player with the highest total.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.text: Write the section of the program that inputs and validates the runs for every player in every match.
parts.answer:
FOR Player ← 1 TO 20
    FOR Match ← 1 TO 10
        OUTPUT "Enter runs for ", PlayerName[Player], " in match ", Match
        INPUT Runs[Player, Match]
        WHILE Runs[Player, Match] < 0 OR Runs[Player, Match] > 300 DO
            OUTPUT "Invalid: runs must be 0 to 300. Re-enter"
            INPUT Runs[Player, Match]
        ENDWHILE
    NEXT Match
NEXT Player

FOR Player ← 1 TO 20

    FOR Match ← 1 TO 10

INPUT Row

    NEXT Seat

NEXT Row
parts.working: 1 mark each: takings output with message; loop through rows; counter reset for each row; counts seats that are FALSE; outputs row number and count.

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A school canteen sells 5 items. The arrays ItemName[1:5] (STRING) and Price[1:5] (REAL) already hold the item names and prices. An array Sold[1:5] of INTEGER will hold the number of each item sold in a day.
Requirements:
• set all values in Sold to 0
• for each order, display a numbered menu, input the item number (1–5) and quantity (1–10) with validation, output the cost of that order and update Sold
• stop taking orders when the item number 9 is entered
• output, for each item, the name, number sold and money taken, and then the total money taken for the day.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that initialises Sold and displays the menu.
parts.answer:
FOR Item ← 1 TO 5

NEXT Item
// menu display (used before each order)

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A public library in Peshawar records returned books. For each of 30 returns in a day, the librarian inputs the member ID (exactly 6 characters) and the number of days late (0 to 60). The fine is Rs 20 per day for the first 7 days late and Rs 50 per day after that; the maximum fine is Rs 2000.
The program uses arrays MemberID[1:30] (STRING) and Fine[1:30] (INTEGER).
Requirements:
• input and validate the member ID (length check) and days late (range check)
• calculate and store each fine and output it
• output the total fines, the average fine of the members who paid a fine (rounded to 2 decimal places), and the member ID with the largest fine.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates the data for return number Count.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Enter 6-character member ID"
INPUT MemberID[Count]
WHILE LENGTH(MemberID[Count]) <> 6 DO
    OUTPUT "ID must be exactly 6 characters. Re-enter"
    INPUT MemberID[Count]
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "Enter days late (0-60)"
INPUT DaysLate
WHILE DaysLate < 0 OR DaysLate > 60 DO
    OUTPUT "Days late must be 0 to 60. Re-enter"
    INPUT DaysLate
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ID input into array; length check using LENGTH() <> 6; re-input loop with message; days late input; range check 0–60 with re-input loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and stores the fine for return number Count.

IF DaysLate <= 7 THEN

ELSE

ENDIF
IF Fine[Count] > 2000 THEN

ENDIF
OUTPUT "Fine for ", MemberID[Count], ": Rs ", Fine[Count]
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: condition DaysLate <= 7; fine = days × 20; fine = 140 + (days − 7) × 50; capped at 2000; output of fine with ID.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the total, the average fine of members who paid a fine, and the member with the largest fine.

Payers ← 0
MaxIndex ← 1
FOR Count ← 1 TO 30

    IF Fine[Count] > Fine[MaxIndex] THEN

OUTPUT "Total fines: Rs ", Total

OUTPUT "Largest fine: ", MemberID[MaxIndex], " Rs ", Fine[MaxIndex]
parts.working: 1 mark each: total accumulated; payers counted only when fine > 0; average = total / payers rounded to 2 d.p. (division by zero avoided); index of largest fine tracked; outputs with messages.

parts.answer: Rs 790 and Rs 2000

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A charity marathon in Lahore has up to 500 runners. Each runner's number (1 to 500) and finishing time in hours, minutes and seconds are input. The program stores the times in seconds in an array Seconds[1:500] of INTEGER; a value of 0 means the runner did not finish.
Requirements:
• set every element of Seconds to 0
• input results until runner number −1 is entered; validate the runner number, minutes and seconds (0–59) and hours (0–7); a runner number that already has a time must be rejected
• output the number of finishers, the runner number of the fastest finisher and the average finishing time as hours, minutes and whole seconds
• output how many finishers completed in under 4 hours.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that initialises the array and inputs and validates all results.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Seconds : ARRAY[1:500] OF INTEGER
FOR R ← 1 TO 500
    Seconds[R] ← 0
NEXT R
OUTPUT "Enter runner number (-1 to finish)"
INPUT Runner
WHILE Runner <> -1 DO
    IF Runner < 1 OR Runner > 500 THEN
        OUTPUT "Invalid runner number"
    ELSE
        IF Seconds[Runner] <> 0 THEN
            OUTPUT "This runner already has a time"
        ELSE
            REPEAT
                OUTPUT "Enter hours, minutes, seconds"
                INPUT H, M, S
            UNTIL H >= 0 AND H <= 7 AND M >= 0 AND M <= 59 AND S >= 0 AND S <= 59
            Seconds[Runner] ← H * 3600 + M * 60 + S
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT "Enter runner number (-1 to finish)"
    INPUT Runner
ENDWHILE
parts.working: 1 mark each for any seven of: array initialised to 0; loop until −1; runner number range checked; duplicate check (Seconds[Runner] <> 0); hours, minutes, seconds input; validation of all three ranges with re-input; conversion H × 3600 + M × 60 + S; stored at Seconds[Runner] and next runner input inside loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and outputs the number of finishers, the fastest runner and the count under 4 hours.
parts.answer:
Finishers ← 0
Total ← 0
Fastest ← 0
Under4 ← 0
FOR R ← 1 TO 500
    IF Seconds[R] > 0 THEN
        Finishers ← Finishers + 1
        Total ← Total + Seconds[R]
        IF Fastest = 0 THEN
            Fastest ← R
        ELSE
            IF Seconds[R] < Seconds[Fastest] THEN
                Fastest ← R
            ENDIF
        ENDIF
        IF Seconds[R] < 4 * 3600 THEN
            Under4 ← Under4 + 1
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
NEXT R
OUTPUT "Finishers: ", Finishers
OUTPUT "Fastest runner: ", Fastest
OUTPUT "Under 4 hours: ", Under4
parts.working: 1 mark each: only times > 0 counted; fastest found correctly (index stored, first finisher handled); under-4-hours test uses 14 400 seconds; outputs with messages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the average finishing time in hours, minutes and whole seconds.
parts.answer:
IF Finishers > 0 THEN
    Avg ← ROUND(Total / Finishers, 0)
    OUTPUT "Average: ", Avg DIV 3600, " h ", (Avg MOD 3600) DIV 60, " min ", Avg MOD 60, " s"
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark each: average = total ÷ finishers rounded to whole seconds (division by zero avoided); hours using DIV 3600; minutes and seconds using MOD/DIV.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The average time is 15 125 seconds. State what your program outputs for the average.
parts.answer: Average: 4 h 12 min 5 s

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A cold-storage warehouse near Okara stores mangoes for export. A temperature reading (°C, REAL) is taken every hour for 7 days and stored in a two-dimensional array Temp[1:7, 1:24]. Safe readings are from 8.0 to 13.0 inclusive.
Requirements:
• input all 168 readings; any reading below −10 or above 40 must be rejected as a sensor fault and re-entered
• for each day output the day number, the lowest and highest reading and the average reading to 1 decimal place
• output the day and hour of every unsafe reading
• output 'SPOILAGE RISK' for any day that has 3 or more consecutive unsafe readings.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates all the readings.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        REPEAT
            OUTPUT "Temperature for day ", Day, " hour ", Hour
            INPUT Temp[Day, Hour]
        UNTIL Temp[Day, Hour] >= -10 AND Temp[Day, Hour] <= 40
    NEXT Hour
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: nested loops 7 × 24; prompt and input to Temp[Day, Hour]; validation −10 to 40; re-input until valid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that outputs each day's lowest, highest and average reading, and the day and hour of every unsafe reading.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    Low ← Temp[Day, 1]
    High ← Temp[Day, 1]
    DayTotal ← 0
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        DayTotal ← DayTotal + Temp[Day, Hour]
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < Low THEN
            Low ← Temp[Day, Hour]
        ENDIF
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] > High THEN
            High ← Temp[Day, Hour]
        ENDIF
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < 8.0 OR Temp[Day, Hour] > 13.0 THEN
            OUTPUT "Unsafe reading on day ", Day, " at hour ", Hour
        ENDIF
    NEXT Hour
    OUTPUT "Day ", Day, " low ", Low, " high ", High, " average ", ROUND(DayTotal / 24, 1)
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: low and high initialised to first reading of the day; sum reset per day; comparisons update low and high; average = sum / 24 rounded to 1 d.p.; unsafe test < 8.0 OR > 13.0; outputs day and hour of unsafe readings; daily output with messages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs 'SPOILAGE RISK' for any day with 3 or more consecutive unsafe readings.
parts.answer:
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
    Run ← 0
    Risk ← FALSE
    FOR Hour ← 1 TO 24
        IF Temp[Day, Hour] < 8.0 OR Temp[Day, Hour] > 13.0 THEN
            Run ← Run + 1
            IF Run >= 3 THEN
                Risk ← TRUE
            ENDIF
        ELSE
            Run ← 0
        ENDIF
    NEXT Hour
    IF Risk = TRUE THEN
        OUTPUT "Day ", Day, ": SPOILAGE RISK"
    ENDIF
NEXT Day
parts.working: 1 mark each: counter of consecutive unsafe readings increased; counter reset to 0 on a safe reading; flag set when counter reaches 3 (output only once per day); output with day number.

stem:
A shopping mall car park in Karachi records the number plate and the time a car entered and left, as whole hours and minutes on a 24-hour clock (the car park is open from 08:00 to 23:00, so every stay is on one day). The charge is Rs 100 for the first hour or part of an hour, then Rs 60 for each extra hour or part of an hour. Cars staying 15 minutes or less park free.
The program processes 200 cars a day, using arrays Plate[1:200] (STRING) and Charge[1:200] (INTEGER).
Requirements:
• input and validate the times (hours 8–23, minutes 0–59, leaving time after entry time)
• calculate the stay in minutes and the charge, and output both
• output the total takings and the number of cars that parked free.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates the entry and exit times for car number Car and calculates the stay in minutes.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Number plate"
INPUT Plate[Car]
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Entry time: hours then minutes"
    INPUT InH, InM
UNTIL InH >= 8 AND InH <= 23 AND InM >= 0 AND InM <= 59
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Exit time: hours then minutes"
    INPUT OutH, OutM

UNTIL OutH >= 8 AND OutH <= 23 AND OutM >= 0 AND OutM <= 59 AND Stay > 0

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and outputs the charge for car number Car.

IF Stay <= 15 THEN
    Charge[Car] ← 0
    FreeCars ← FreeCars + 1
ELSE
    Hours ← Stay DIV 60
    IF Stay MOD 60 > 0 THEN
        Hours ← Hours + 1          // part of an hour counts as a whole hour
    ENDIF
    Charge[Car] ← 100 + (Hours − 1) * 60

OUTPUT Plate[Car], " stayed ", Stay, " minutes, charge Rs ", Charge[Car]
parts.working: 1 mark each: free if stay ≤ 15 and free counter increased; hours rounded up using DIV/MOD; charge = 100 + (hours − 1) × 60; stored in Charge[Car]; output with plate and stay.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the main loop and the end-of-day output. Initialise any totals.

FreeCars ← 0
FOR Car ← 1 TO 200

    // section (b)

NEXT Car
OUTPUT "Total takings: Rs ", Total
OUTPUT "Cars parked free: ", FreeCars

parts.text: A car enters at 10:40 and leaves at 13:05. Calculate its charge.
parts.answer: Rs 220

stem:
A teacher in Quetta gives a 20-question multiple-choice quiz to a class of 35 students. Each answer is a single character A, B, C or D.
The program uses:
• Key[1:20] (CHAR) holding the correct answers, already filled
• Answers[1:35, 1:20] (CHAR) for the students' answers
• StudentName[1:35] (STRING), already filled
Requirements:
• input every student's answers; accept lower-case letters by converting them to upper case; reject anything other than A–D
• calculate each student's score out of 20 and output the name, score and grade (Distinction 17 or more, Merit 13–16, Pass 10–12, otherwise Fail)
• output the question number(s) answered correctly by the fewest students.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates all answers.
parts.answer:
FOR S ← 1 TO 35
    FOR Qn ← 1 TO 20
        REPEAT
            OUTPUT StudentName[S], " answer to question ", Qn
            INPUT Ans
            Ans ← UCASE(Ans)
        UNTIL Ans = "A" OR Ans = "B" OR Ans = "C" OR Ans = "D"
        Answers[S, Qn] ← Ans
    NEXT Qn
NEXT S
parts.working: 1 mark each: nested loops 35 × 20; input with prompt; conversion with UCASE; validation only A–D with re-input; stored in Answers[S, Qn].

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that calculates and outputs each student's score and grade, and counts how many students got each question right in an array Correct[1:20].
parts.answer:
FOR Qn ← 1 TO 20
    Correct[Qn] ← 0
NEXT Qn
FOR S ← 1 TO 35
    Score ← 0
    FOR Qn ← 1 TO 20
        IF Answers[S, Qn] = Key[Qn] THEN
            Score ← Score + 1
            Correct[Qn] ← Correct[Qn] + 1
        ENDIF
    NEXT Qn
    IF Score >= 17 THEN
        Grade ← "Distinction"
    ELSE
        IF Score >= 13 THEN
            Grade ← "Merit"
        ELSE
            IF Score >= 10 THEN
                Grade ← "Pass"
            ELSE
                Grade ← "Fail"
            ENDIF
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT StudentName[S], " ", Score, "/20 ", Grade
NEXT S
parts.working: 1 mark each: Correct array initialised; score reset for each student; compare Answers[S, Qn] with Key[Qn]; score and Correct[Qn] incremented; grade boundaries correct; output name, score and grade.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the question number(s) answered correctly by the fewest students.
parts.answer:
Fewest ← Correct[1]
FOR Qn ← 2 TO 20
    IF Correct[Qn] < Fewest THEN
        Fewest ← Correct[Qn]
    ENDIF
NEXT Qn
OUTPUT "Hardest question(s):"
FOR Qn ← 1 TO 20
    IF Correct[Qn] = Fewest THEN
        OUTPUT Qn
    ENDIF
NEXT Qn
parts.working: 1 mark each: minimum initialised; loop finds minimum; second loop finds all questions equal to minimum (handles ties); output with message.

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A pharmacy in Multan keeps 40 medicines. The arrays MedName[1:40] (STRING), Stock[1:40] (INTEGER) and ReorderLevel[1:40] (INTEGER) are already filled.
Requirements:
• display a menu: 1 Record a sale, 2 Record a delivery, 3 Reorder report, 4 Exit
• for a sale or delivery, input the medicine name and search for it; if it is not found output a message; otherwise input the quantity (must be a positive whole number; a sale cannot be more than the stock) and update Stock
• the reorder report lists every medicine whose stock is at or below its reorder level, and the number of such medicines
• repeat until option 4 is chosen.
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs a medicine name and performs a linear search, setting Found to the index of the medicine or to 0 if it is not found.
parts.answer:
OUTPUT "Enter medicine name"
INPUT SearchName
Found ← 0
Index ← 1
WHILE Found = 0 AND Index <= 40 DO
    IF MedName[Index] = SearchName THEN
        Found ← Index
    ENDIF
    Index ← Index + 1
ENDWHILE
IF Found = 0 THEN
    OUTPUT "Medicine not found"
ENDIF
parts.working: 1 mark each: name input; loop through array stopping when found or end reached; comparison with MedName[Index] and Found set to index; not-found message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that processes a sale (option 1) once the medicine has been found.
parts.answer:
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Quantity sold"
    INPUT Qty
UNTIL Qty > 0 AND Qty = ROUND(Qty, 0) AND Qty <= Stock[Found]
Stock[Found] ← Stock[Found] − Qty
OUTPUT MedName[Found], " stock now ", Stock[Found]
parts.working: 1 mark each: quantity input; checks positive and whole; checks not greater than Stock[Found]; stock reduced and new level output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the menu loop, including option 2 (delivery) and option 3 (reorder report). You may refer to your sections (a) and (b).
parts.answer:
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "1 Record a sale  2 Record a delivery  3 Reorder report  4 Exit"
    INPUT Option
    CASE OF Option
        1 : // section (a); IF Found <> 0 THEN section (b)
        2 : // section (a)
            IF Found <> 0 THEN
                REPEAT
                    OUTPUT "Quantity delivered"
                    INPUT Qty
                UNTIL Qty > 0 AND Qty = ROUND(Qty, 0)
                Stock[Found] ← Stock[Found] + Qty
            ENDIF
        3 : Count ← 0
            FOR M ← 1 TO 40
                IF Stock[M] <= ReorderLevel[M] THEN
                    OUTPUT MedName[M], " stock ", Stock[M]
                    Count ← Count + 1
                ENDIF
            NEXT M
            OUTPUT Count, " medicines need reordering"
        4 : OUTPUT "Goodbye"
        OTHERWISE OUTPUT "Invalid option"
    ENDCASE
UNTIL Option = 4
parts.working: 1 mark each: menu output and option input inside a loop ending at 4; selection (CASE or IF) on option; delivery validated positive whole number; stock increased; report loop compares Stock[M] <= ReorderLevel[M]; outputs names and count; invalid option handled.

stem:
A fitness club in Kuala Lumpur gives each member a step counter. For one member, the steps taken each day for 4 weeks are stored in a two-dimensional array Steps[1:4, 1:7] of INTEGER (week, day).
Requirements:

• output the total steps for each week and the week with the most steps
• output the number of days on which the member reached the target of 10 000 steps, and the percentage of days (to 1 decimal place).
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the section that inputs and validates the steps.

FOR Week ← 1 TO 4
    FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
        OUTPUT "Steps for week ", Week, " day ", Day

parts.text: Write the section that outputs each week's total and the week with the most steps.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the section that outputs the number and percentage of days on which 10 000 steps were reached.

subtopic: Extended programming task (15-mark scenario)
stem:
A metro bus route in Lahore has 15 stops, numbered 1 to 15. The fare depends on the number of stops travelled: 1–4 stops Rs 30, 5–9 stops Rs 50, 10 or more stops Rs 70. Students pay half fare (rounded down to a whole rupee).
The program records journeys during one day using a two-dimensional array Trips[1:15, 1:15] of INTEGER, where Trips[Board, Leave] counts journeys from stop Board to stop Leave.
Requirements:
• initialise every element of Trips to 0
• for each journey, input the boarding stop, the leaving stop (both 1–15 and different) and whether the passenger is a student (Y/N); output the fare and update Trips and the day's takings
• stop when 0 is entered as the boarding stop
• output the total takings, the number of student journeys, and the busiest journey (the boarding and leaving stops with the highest count).
You may answer in pseudocode or a high-level programming language. Use meaningful identifiers and add comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a function Fare(Board : INTEGER, Leave : INTEGER, Student : BOOLEAN) RETURNS INTEGER that returns the fare for one journey.
parts.answer:
FUNCTION Fare(Board : INTEGER, Leave : INTEGER, Student : BOOLEAN) RETURNS INTEGER
    DECLARE Stops, Cost : INTEGER
    Stops ← Board − Leave
    IF Stops < 0 THEN
        Stops ← -Stops               // travel in either direction
    ENDIF
    IF Stops <= 4 THEN
        Cost ← 30
    ELSE
        IF Stops <= 9 THEN
            Cost ← 50
        ELSE
            Cost ← 70
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    IF Student = TRUE THEN
        Cost ← Cost DIV 2
    ENDIF
    RETURN Cost
ENDFUNCTION
parts.working: 1 mark each: function header with parameters and return type; number of stops as a positive difference; correct fare bands; half fare using DIV 2 for students; value returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the section that initialises Trips and processes journeys until 0 is entered.
parts.answer:
FOR F ← 1 TO 15
    FOR T ← 1 TO 15
        Trips[F, T] ← 0
    NEXT T
NEXT F
Takings ← 0
StudentTrips ← 0
OUTPUT "Boarding stop (0 to finish)"
INPUT Board
WHILE Board <> 0 DO
    IF Board >= 1 AND Board <= 15 THEN
        REPEAT
            OUTPUT "Leaving stop"
            INPUT Leave
        UNTIL Leave >= 1 AND Leave <= 15 AND Leave <> Board
        REPEAT
            OUTPUT "Student? Y/N"
            INPUT Reply
        UNTIL Reply = "Y" OR Reply = "N"
        IsStudent ← (Reply = "Y")
        IF IsStudent THEN
            StudentTrips ← StudentTrips + 1
        ENDIF
        Cost ← Fare(Board, Leave, IsStudent)
        OUTPUT "Fare: Rs ", Cost
        Takings ← Takings + Cost
        Trips[Board, Leave] ← Trips[Board, Leave] + 1
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Invalid stop"
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT "Boarding stop (0 to finish)"

PROCEDURE SaveWeek()
    DECLARE Value, Total : REAL
    OPENFILE "week.txt" FOR WRITE
    FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
        WRITEFILE "week.txt", Sales[Day]
    NEXT Day
    CLOSEFILE "week.txt"
    Total ← 0
    OPENFILE "week.txt" FOR READ

    NEXT Day
    CLOSEFILE "week.txt"
    OUTPUT "Week total: ", Total

For customers: a compiler, because it produces an executable that runs without a translator on the customer's device and runs faster.
parts.working: 1 mark interpreter for development + 1 mark reason; 1 mark compiler for customers + 1 mark reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why giving customers the compiled version also protects the company's work.
parts.answer: Customers only receive the executable machine code, not the source code, so they cannot easily read, copy or change the program.
parts.working: 1 mark: source code is not distributed so it cannot be copied/modified.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A drone's flight controller has a small amount of memory and must respond to its sensors very quickly. Explain why its designers might write parts of the control program in assembly language instead of a high-level language.
parts.answer: Assembly gives direct control of the hardware (registers, memory addresses, ports), needed to read the sensors and drive the motors; each instruction translates to one machine code instruction, so the code can be written to be compact, which suits the small memory; the programmer can optimise the code so it executes faster, which suits the need for quick response.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 for each point and 1 for each linked expansion (direct hardware control; compact code for small memory; fast execution for quick response).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same assembly language program could not be used on a drone that has a different type of processor.
parts.answer: Assembly language is specific to a processor's instruction set, so a different processor would need a rewritten program.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's program contains two syntax errors, one on line 14 and one on line 30. Describe what happens when the program is translated with an interpreter.
parts.answer: Lines 1 to 13 are translated and executed; the interpreter stops at line 14 and reports that error; the error on line 30 is not reported until line 14 has been corrected and the program is re-run to that point.
parts.working: 1 mark: runs until line 14 then stops and reports it. 1 mark: line 30 error only found after correcting line 14 and running again.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens when the same program is translated with a compiler.
parts.answer: The compiler attempts to translate the whole program; it reports both errors (lines 14 and 30) in an error list at the end; no executable file is produced, so none of the program runs.
parts.working: 1 mark: both errors reported together after translation. 1 mark: no executable produced / program does not run.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A team in Dubai is building an appointment-booking system for a hospital. Explain how three different features of an IDE would help the team produce working, maintainable code.
parts.working: For each of three features: 1 mark for naming/describing the feature, 1 mark for explaining how it helps in this team context.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Low-level languages include machine code and assembly language. Explain why a programmer would prefer to write in assembly language rather than machine code.
parts.answer: Assembly uses mnemonics instead of binary, so it is easier to read, write and remember; errors are easier to find and correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: mnemonics rather than binary / easier to understand. 1 mark: easier to debug / fewer mistakes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why most application programs are written in a high-level language rather than assembly language.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. English-like statements are quicker to write and easier to debug; it is machine independent so it can run on different processors after translation; one statement can do the work of many machine instructions; more programmers know high-level languages, so it is easier to maintain.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a task for which assembly language would be chosen.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. writing a device driver; programming an embedded controller with little memory; code that must directly manipulate a hardware register; a time-critical routine.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Programming languages, translators and IDEs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A translation app has two versions: one is interpreted and one is compiled. Both are run on the same phone. Explain why the interpreted version runs more slowly.
parts.answer: Each line must be translated every time it is executed (including every time a loop repeats), so translation time is added to run time; the compiled version has already been translated to machine code, so it executes directly.
parts.working: 1 mark: interpreter translates each line as it runs / repeatedly. 1 mark: compiled code is already machine code so no translation at run time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two things that a user must have on the phone to run the interpreted version but does not need for the compiled version.
parts.answer: The interpreter (translation software) and the source code of the program.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify whether each of the following is system software or application software.
1. Operating system
2. Word processor
3. Anti-virus utility
4. Photo-editing program
5. Device driver for a printer
6. Spreadsheet
parts.answer: System: 1, 3, 5. Application: 2, 4, 6.
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct (6 correct = 3 marks).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three functions of an operating system.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. managing files; handling interrupts; providing a user interface; managing peripherals and drivers; managing memory; managing multitasking; providing a platform for running applications; providing system security; managing user accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark for each function.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between system software and application software.
parts.answer: System software provides the services the computer needs to run/operate and manage the hardware, and a platform for other software; application software lets the user carry out specific tasks they want to do.
parts.working: 1 mark for system software description, 1 mark for application software description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of software. Do not use brand names.
parts.answer: System: e.g. operating system, utility such as anti-virus, device driver. Application: e.g. word processor, web browser, spreadsheet, game, photo editor.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct example. Brand names score 0.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A delivery rider in Lahore uses a smartphone. The maps app is open while music plays and a messaging app receives a new order. Explain how the operating system manages memory and multitasking so that all three apps can run.
parts.answer:
Memory management: the OS allocates each app its own area of memory and keeps track of it; it prevents one app from using/overwriting another app's memory; it frees memory when an app is closed.
Multitasking: the OS shares processor time between the apps, switching rapidly between them so they appear to run at the same time; it decides priorities (e.g. the messaging alert).
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for memory management points and up to 2 marks for multitasking points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher connects a new printer to a classroom computer. Explain how the operating system manages this peripheral.
parts.answer: The OS uses/installs a device driver for the printer so that it can communicate with it; it sends data to the printer and manages the print queue (spooling); it handles interrupts/signals from the printer, e.g. out of paper.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the operating system provides a user interface for the teacher.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. a graphical user interface with windows, icons, menus and a pointer; a command-line interface.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A laptop needs hardware, firmware, an operating system and applications. Put these four layers in order, starting with the layer closest to the hardware.
parts.answer: Hardware → firmware → operating system → applications
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of firmware such as the bootloader when the laptop is switched on.
parts.answer: Firmware is stored in ROM/non-volatile memory, so it is available when power is switched on; the bootloader runs first and loads the operating system into RAM/starts the OS.
parts.working: 1 mark: stored in ROM/non-volatile memory. 1 mark: loads/starts the operating system.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why applications are run by the operating system rather than directly on the hardware.
parts.answer: The OS provides a platform/standard services so applications do not need to manage the hardware themselves, and it controls their access to the hardware.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital uses computers that store patient records. Explain how three functions of the operating system help the computers to run safely and correctly in this hospital.
parts.working: For each of three functions: 1 mark for the function, 1 mark for an explanation applied to the hospital.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer has 4 GiB of RAM. A student opens several large programs at once. Explain how the operating system manages the processes and memory so the student can keep working.
parts.answer: The OS allocates memory to each process and keeps a record of which memory each uses; when RAM is full it can move data/pages not currently needed to virtual memory on secondary storage; it swaps them back into RAM when needed; it schedules processor time between the processes (multitasking) so each makes progress; it frees memory when a program is closed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student notices that the computer slows down a lot when very many programs are open. Explain why.
parts.answer: RAM is full so more data is held in virtual memory; data must be repeatedly swapped between RAM and secondary storage, which is much slower than RAM (disk thrashing).
parts.working: 1 mark: virtual memory/secondary storage used. 1 mark: swapping data is slow compared with RAM.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: System and application software, operating system functions

parts.label: a
parts.text: A games company says its new game 'needs an operating system to run'. Explain why application software depends on an operating system.
parts.answer: The OS provides the platform on which the application runs; it gives access to the hardware (screen, keyboard, sound) through drivers, so the game does not need its own code for each device; it allocates memory and processor time to the game; it handles files such as saved games.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same game file may not run on a computer with a different operating system.
parts.answer: The game is written to use the services/instructions provided by one particular operating system; another OS provides different services/file formats, so the game cannot call them correctly.
parts.working: 1 mark: relies on the specific OS services. 1 mark: a different OS works differently so the calls fail.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an interrupt.
parts.answer: A signal sent to the processor from a device or from software, telling it that something needs attention/processing.
parts.working: 1 mark: a signal to the processor. 1 mark: from hardware or software indicating it needs attention.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a hardware interrupt and one example of a software interrupt.
parts.answer: Hardware: e.g. a key being pressed, the mouse being moved, a printer running out of paper. Software: e.g. division by zero, two processes trying to use the same memory location, a program requesting input.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct example.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a processor handles an interrupt.
parts.answer: The interrupt is placed in a queue/stored according to its priority; at the end of each fetch-decode-execute cycle the processor checks for interrupts; if the interrupt has a higher priority than the current task, the current task is suspended; the current state/register values are saved (on the stack); the interrupt service routine (ISR) for that interrupt is called/run; when the ISR is finished, the saved state is restored and the original task continues.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Interrupts

parts.label: a
parts.text: Asad is listening to music on his computer while a document prints. At the same moment he presses a key and the printer runs out of paper. Explain how the processor uses interrupts to deal with both events without the music stopping for long.
parts.answer: Each device sends an interrupt signal; the interrupts are queued according to priority; at the end of each FDE cycle the processor checks the queue; it saves the state of the current task, runs the ISR for the highest-priority interrupt, then for the next one (e.g. shows an out-of-paper message, reads the key press); after each ISR the saved state is restored so the music program continues; this happens so fast the music continues smoothly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four points applied to the scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why using interrupts is more efficient than the processor repeatedly checking every device to see whether it needs attention.
parts.answer: The processor does not waste time checking devices that do not need attention; it can carry on with other processing and only responds when a device sends an interrupt.
parts.working: 1 mark: no time wasted polling idle devices. 1 mark: processor continues useful work and responds only when signalled.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
parts.answer: The internet is the global network of interconnected networks/computers (the infrastructure); the World Wide Web is the collection of websites and web pages that are accessed using the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark for internet = network infrastructure. 1 mark for WWW = web pages/websites accessed over the internet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the language in which web pages are written so that a browser can display them.
parts.answer: HTML (HyperText Markup Language)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.text:
A parent types this URL to find school fees:
https://www.greenvalleyschool.edu.pk/admissions/fees.html
Identify the protocol, the domain name and the web page/file name in this URL.
parts.answer:
Protocol: https
Domain name: www.greenvalleyschool.edu.pk (accept greenvalleyschool.edu.pk)
File name: fees.html
parts.working: 1 mark for each part identified correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what /admissions/ represents in the URL.
parts.answer: The folder/directory (path) on the web server where the page is stored.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a session cookie and a persistent cookie.
parts.answer: A session cookie is stored temporarily (in memory) and is deleted when the browser is closed; a persistent cookie is saved on the user's storage and remains until its expiry date or until the user deletes it.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of cookies.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. storing items in a virtual shopping basket; saving login details so the user stays logged in; remembering user preferences such as language; tracking pages visited to show targeted adverts; storing the progress through a website.
parts.working: 1 mark for each use.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three functions of a web browser.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. renders/displays HTML as web pages; stores bookmarks/favourites; records user history; allows use of multiple tabs; stores and manages cookies; provides navigation tools (back, forward, refresh); has an address bar; sends requests for web pages using HTTP/HTTPS; runs scripts such as JavaScript.
parts.working: 1 mark for each function.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zainab types the URL of an online newspaper into her browser. Describe how the Domain Name Server (DNS) is used so that the web page can be found and displayed.
parts.answer: The browser sends the domain name/URL to a DNS server; the DNS server looks up the domain name in its database to find the matching IP address; if it does not have it, it passes the request to another DNS server (higher in the hierarchy); the IP address is returned to the browser; the browser uses the IP address to send a request to the web server; the web server sends the web page (HTML) back; the browser renders it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five points in a logical order.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online clothing shop uses HTTPS instead of HTTP. Explain the difference between HTTP and HTTPS.
parts.answer: Both are protocols used to transfer web pages between server and browser; HTTPS is secure – it uses SSL/TLS to encrypt the data sent, whereas HTTP data is not encrypted.
parts.working: 1 mark: both are protocols for transferring web pages / rules for communication. 1 mark: HTTPS encrypts using SSL/TLS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that the shop uses HTTPS when customers pay.
parts.answer: Card and personal details are encrypted, so if the data is intercepted it cannot be understood; it also confirms (via the certificate) that the customer is connected to the genuine shop server.
parts.working: 1 mark: data encrypted / meaningless if intercepted. 1 mark: payment details protected / authenticity of website.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online bookshop in Peshawar uses cookies. Bilal adds three books to his basket, closes the browser by mistake, then opens the site again the next day. His basket still contains the books and he is still logged in. Explain how cookies have made this possible.
parts.answer: The website stored a cookie (a small text file) on Bilal's computer; it was a persistent cookie, so it was not deleted when the browser closed; it contained/identified his basket items and login details; when he returned, the browser sent the cookie to the website, which read it and restored his basket and session.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a session cookie could not have done this.
parts.answer: A session cookie is deleted when the browser is closed, so the basket and login information would have been lost.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A web browser has many functions. Describe how each of these helps a user.
(i) Bookmarks
(ii) History
(iii) Tabs
(iv) Address bar
parts.answer:
(i) Bookmarks save the address of a favourite page so it can be opened again quickly.
(ii) History records the pages visited, so the user can find and return to a page they saw earlier.
(iii) Tabs let several web pages be open at the same time in one window and switched between.
(iv) The address bar lets the user type a URL to go directly to a web page (and shows the current page's URL).
parts.working: 1 mark for each description.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'A URL and an IP address are the same thing.' Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: A URL is a text-based address of a web page/resource that is easy for humans to remember; an IP address is a numeric address that identifies a device (the web server) on the network.
parts.working: 1 mark for URL description. 1 mark for IP address description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why websites use URLs even though computers use IP addresses to find web servers.
parts.answer: URLs (domain names) are easier for people to remember and type than a string of numbers; DNS converts the domain name into the IP address, so the web server's IP address can change without the URL changing.
parts.working: 1 mark: easier to remember. 1 mark: DNS converts to IP / IP can change while URL stays the same.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a web page is requested, located and displayed when a user types a URL into a web browser. Your answer should refer to the browser, DNS, IP address, web server, HTTP/HTTPS and HTML.
parts.answer: The user types the URL into the address bar of the browser; the browser sends the domain name to a DNS server; DNS looks up / finds the matching IP address (asking other DNS servers if needed); the IP address is sent back to the browser; the browser sends an HTTP/HTTPS request to the web server at that IP address; the web server sends the web page files (HTML) back using HTTP/HTTPS; the browser renders the HTML and displays the page (and may store cookies).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six points in a logical sequence.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sports news website uses persistent cookies to personalise the stories it shows. Explain how a persistent cookie allows the website to personalise the stories.
parts.answer: The cookie stores data such as the user's preferences and the pages/stories they have viewed; it remains on the user's device between visits; when the user returns, the browser sends the cookie to the website, which reads it and shows stories that match the stored preferences (e.g. their favourite team).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why some users delete persistent cookies, and one consequence of doing so.
parts.answer:
Reasons (any two): privacy concerns about their browsing being tracked; to stop targeted adverts; to protect stored login details on a shared computer; to free storage.
Consequence (any one): preferences are lost/have to be set again; the user must log in again; saved basket items are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason (max 2), 1 mark for a consequence.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs, browsers, HTTP(S), DNS and cookies

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user in Quetta types the domain name of a small travel website. The first DNS server contacted does not have this domain name in its database. Describe what happens next until the browser receives a result.
parts.answer: The DNS server passes/forwards the request to another DNS server (higher up the hierarchy); this continues until a DNS server that holds the domain name is found; that server sends the IP address back (through the chain) to the browser. If no DNS server has the domain name, an error message is returned to the browser (e.g. the site cannot be found).
parts.working: 1 mark: request forwarded to another DNS server. 1 mark: IP address found and returned to browser. 1 mark: error returned if domain not found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the result of the look-up is often stored by the DNS server or browser for a short time.
parts.answer: So that the next request for the same domain can be answered quickly without asking other DNS servers again.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small office in Hyderabad installs a firewall between its network and the internet. State three things the firewall does.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. monitors incoming and outgoing traffic; checks traffic against a set of rules/criteria; blocks traffic that does not meet the rules; can block access to specified websites/IP addresses; can log/record traffic; can alert the user to suspicious traffic; helps prevent hacking/malware entering.
parts.working: 1 mark for each function.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop in Quetta keeps its sales records on one computer. Describe what is meant by a backup.
parts.answer: A copy of the data stored separately (on another device or location) so it can be restored if the original is lost or damaged.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the shop should keep its backup in a different location, for example in cloud storage.
parts.answer: If the shop's computer is damaged, stolen or destroyed (e.g. by fire or flood), a backup kept in the same place could be lost too; an off-site/cloud backup will still be available to restore the data.
parts.working: 1 mark: same event could destroy both copies. 1 mark: off-site copy survives so data can be restored.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online banking app uses two-step verification. Describe how two-step verification works.
parts.answer: The user first enters their password/username; then a second step is needed, such as a one-time code sent to their registered phone or email, which must be entered before access is given.
parts.working: 1 mark: password entered first. 1 mark: second code/factor sent to another device must also be entered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of biometric authentication and one drawback of biometric methods.
parts.answer: Example: fingerprint, face recognition, iris/retina scan, voice recognition. Drawback (any one): can fail if the body part is injured/dirty or in poor light; biometric data cannot be changed if it is stolen; equipment can be expensive.
parts.working: 1 mark for example, 1 mark for drawback.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how SSL (Secure Socket Layer) is used to set up a secure connection between a web browser and a web server.
parts.answer: The browser requests a secure connection from the web server; the browser asks the server to identify itself; the server sends a copy of its digital/SSL certificate (which includes its public key); the browser checks the certificate is authentic/valid (issued by a trusted authority); if valid, the browser sends a message to the server (acknowledgement); the server and browser agree encryption and a secure session begins; data sent is then encrypted.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college network uses both a firewall and a proxy server. Describe two differences between what a firewall does and what a proxy server does.
parts.answer: Any two pairs, e.g. a firewall checks/filters traffic against rules and blocks it, whereas a proxy server acts as an intermediary that makes requests to web servers on behalf of the user; a proxy hides the user's IP address from web servers, a firewall does not; a proxy can cache (store) web pages to speed up later requests, a firewall does not; a firewall can be software on the computer as well as hardware, a proxy is a separate server that the requests pass through.
parts.working: For each difference, 1 mark for the firewall point and 1 mark for the matching proxy point.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school database holds students' names, marks and medical notes. Explain how access levels can be used to protect this data.
parts.answer: Different users are given different access rights depending on their role; e.g. teachers can view and edit marks but cannot see medical notes, while the nurse can view medical notes; students can only view their own marks/read-only; this means users can only see or change the data they need, reducing accidental or deliberate misuse.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points, at least one applied to the school context.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how anti-malware software protects a computer.
parts.answer: It scans files/data (when downloaded/opened or on a schedule); it compares them against a database of known malware (signatures); it can use heuristic checking to spot suspicious behaviour; infected files are quarantined or deleted; it can warn the user.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the anti-malware software should be set to update automatically.
parts.answer: New malware is created all the time, so the database of known malware must be kept up to date to detect it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank in Karachi is launching an online banking website. Identify three different security solutions the bank should use and explain how each one protects customers.
parts.working: For each of three solutions: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for explaining how it protects customers.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university network sends all web requests through a proxy server. Explain how the proxy server improves both the speed and the security of web access for students.
parts.answer:
Speed: the proxy caches web pages that have been requested; when another student requests the same page it is sent from the cache rather than from the internet, so it loads faster and reduces internet traffic.
Security: web servers only see the proxy's IP address, so students' devices are hidden from attackers; the proxy can filter/block requests to unsafe or banned websites; attacks such as DDoS hit the proxy rather than the university's servers.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for speed, up to 2 marks for security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The proxy server cannot stop a student's laptop from being infected by a virus on a USB flash drive. Name a security solution that would.
parts.answer: Anti-malware / anti-virus software on the laptop.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Security solutions (SSL, firewalls, proxy servers, backups)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sana receives an email that appears to come from her mobile network company. It asks her to log in using a link. Describe three checks Sana could make to decide whether the email and website are genuine.

parts.answer: Malicious code is installed on the user's computer or a DNS server is altered, so the user is redirected to a fake website even when they type the correct URL; it is harder to notice because the user has not clicked any suspicious link – the address they typed looks correct.

parts.answer: The attacker infects many computers with malware to create a botnet; the attacker instructs the botnet computers to send very large numbers of requests to the results web server at the same time; the server/network cannot handle all the requests; it slows down or crashes, so genuine students cannot access the results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a brute-force attack on a user's account.
parts.answer: An attacker tries many different passwords one after another, (often using software to try every combination or a list of common passwords) until the correct one is found.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeatedly trying passwords. 1 mark: systematically/automatically until correct one found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways a website can reduce the risk of a successful brute-force attack.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. require strong passwords (long, mix of letters, numbers and symbols); lock the account after a set number of failed attempts; use two-step verification; add a delay between attempts.

subtopic: Cyber security threats

parts.label: a
parts.text: A traveller connects to free Wi-Fi at an airport and logs in to an email account that does not use encryption. Describe how data interception could take place.
parts.answer: An attacker uses a packet sniffer (or a fake Wi-Fi access point) to monitor data sent over the network; the data packets are intercepted/copied as they travel between the traveller's device and the server; the attacker examines the packets to read the username, password and messages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how encryption reduces the impact of data interception.
parts.answer: The data is encrypted before it is sent, so if it is intercepted it is meaningless/cannot be understood; only the intended receiver has the key to decrypt it. (Encryption does not stop interception.)
parts.working: 1 mark: intercepted data cannot be understood. 1 mark: only receiver with the key can decrypt / it does not prevent interception itself.

parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this type of threat can succeed even when the company has a firewall and anti-malware software.
parts.answer: It targets people rather than the technology; the worker is manipulated (e.g. by urgency, fear or trust in authority) into giving the password voluntarily, so the attacker logs in as a legitimate user and the technical defences are not triggered.
parts.working: 1 mark: exploits human behaviour/trust. 1 mark: attacker gets genuine credentials so firewall/anti-malware cannot detect it.

parts.answer: Any two, e.g. train staff never to give passwords to anyone, including IT staff; have a policy to verify callers by calling back on a known number; use two-step verification so a password alone is not enough; report suspicious calls.
parts.working: 1 mark for each suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a digital currency.
parts.answer: A currency that exists only in electronic/digital form (it has no physical coins or notes); it can be used to pay for goods and services and is transferred electronically between users.
parts.working: 1 mark: exists only digitally. 1 mark: used/transferred electronically to make payments.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how blockchain is used to record digital currency transactions.
parts.answer: Each transaction is stored in a block with a time-stamp; each block contains the hash value of the previous block, so the blocks are linked in a chain; copies of the blockchain are stored on many computers in a decentralised network; new transactions are added to every copy and none can be removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Digital currency and blockchain

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charity in Lahore is considering using a blockchain to record donations. Explain why it is very difficult for someone to change an earlier record in a blockchain without being detected.
parts.answer: Each block contains its own hash value and the hash of the previous block; changing data in a block changes its hash; this no longer matches the 'previous hash' stored in the next block, so the chain is broken and the change is detected; to hide the change every following block would have to be changed; and because many computers hold copies of the chain, the altered copy would not match the others and would be rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit to the charity's donors of using a blockchain.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. donations are transparent and can be checked by anyone; records cannot be secretly altered, so donors can trust how money is recorded.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The array Cities[1:10] holds the names of 10 cities. Write pseudocode for an efficient bubble sort that puts the names into alphabetical order. The sort must stop as soon as a pass is completed with no swaps.
parts.answer:
DECLARE Cities : ARRAY[1:10] OF STRING
DECLARE Temp : STRING
DECLARE Index, Top : INTEGER
DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
Top ← 9
REPEAT
   Swapped ← FALSE
   FOR Index ← 1 TO Top
      IF Cities[Index] > Cities[Index + 1] THEN
         Temp ← Cities[Index]
         Cities[Index] ← Cities[Index + 1]
         Cities[Index + 1] ← Temp
         Swapped ← TRUE
      ENDIF
   NEXT Index
   Top ← Top - 1
UNTIL Swapped = FALSE OR Top = 0
parts.working: 1 mark: outer loop. 1 mark: inner loop over adjacent pairs without going past element 10. 1 mark: correct comparison of adjacent elements. 1 mark: swap using a temporary variable. 1 mark: flag set to FALSE at start of each pass and TRUE on a swap. 1 mark: outer loop ends when no swaps (accept also reducing the range each pass).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the address 3FA to denary. Show your working.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State, in hexadecimal, the address of the next memory location after 3FA.
parts.answer: 3FB
parts.working: B1: 3FB.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one reason why the engineer reads memory addresses in hexadecimal rather than in binary.
parts.answer: Hexadecimal is shorter and easier to read and remember than a long binary string, so mistakes are less likely (each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so it converts easily back to binary).
parts.working: 1 mark for any one of: shorter / fewer digits; easier for humans to read, remember or type; fewer errors when copying; converts directly to binary (1 digit = 4 bits).

subtopic: HTML structure and presentation
stem: The webmaster of a school in Quetta is building a notice page for the school website using HTML.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the structure of a web page written in HTML.
parts.answer: The structure is the layout and content of the page: which elements it contains (headings, paragraphs, images, links, tables) and where they appear.
parts.working: 1 mark for: the layout / content / elements of the page and where they are placed (e.g. headings, paragraphs, images).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the presentation of a web page.
parts.answer: The presentation is the formatting or style of the content, for example its colours, fonts and text sizes.
parts.working: 1 mark for: how the content looks / its formatting or style (colour, font, size, background).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two examples of presentation that the webmaster could set for the school's notice page.
parts.answer: Any two of: the background colour; the font (typeface) of the text; the text size; the colour of the headings; borders or spacing around elements.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid presentation features (colour, font, font size, background, border, alignment/spacing).

parts.label: d
parts.text:
For each change below, state whether it changes the structure or the presentation of the notice page.
(i) A new paragraph giving the date of the sports day is added.
(ii) The headings are made larger and changed to dark blue.
parts.answer:
(i) Structure
(ii) Presentation
parts.working: 1 mark each: (i) structure – new content/element added to the page; (ii) presentation – only the size and colour (style) of existing content change.

stem:
Part of the HTML file for the home page of an online shop in Karachi is shown below. Line numbers are given for reference only. 1 2 3 Bazaar Deals 4 5 6 7

subtopic: Ethics and software licensing
stem: Mehwish downloads a photo-editing program for her laptop. The program is shareware.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by copyright.
parts.answer: Copyright is the legal right of the creator (owner) of a work, such as a program, to control how it is copied, used and distributed.
parts.working: 1 mark: legal protection / right of the owner or creator to stop others copying or distributing the work without permission.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by shareware.
parts.answer: Shareware is software that users can try free of charge for a limited trial period (or with some features disabled). To keep using it, or to unlock all features, the user must pay for a licence. It is still protected by copyright and the source code is not supplied, so users may not modify it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: free to try / free trial; limited time or limited features; must pay (register / buy a licence) to continue or get full version; protected by copyright; source code not available / cannot be modified.

stem: Freeware and free software are two different ways of distributing programs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each statement, write whether it applies to freeware only, free software only, both, or neither.
(i) The user may study and change the source code.
(ii) The program is protected by copyright.
(iii) The user must pay once a 30-day trial has ended.
(iv) The source code is normally not supplied to the user.
parts.answer:
(i) Free software only

parts.text: A programmer in Nairobi releases a mobile app for farmers as free software. Explain one benefit to the programmer of doing this.
parts.answer: Other programmers can read and improve the source code, so bugs are found and fixed and new features are added at no cost to her, making the app better (and more widely used).

subtopic: Ethics and software licensing
stem: A software company in Lahore sells an accounting program to shops. It finds that unlicensed copies of the program are being used in many markets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by software piracy.
parts.answer: Copying, distributing or using software without the permission of the copyright owner (without a valid licence).
parts.working: 1 mark: illegal copying / use / distribution of software without a licence or permission.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three methods the software company could use to reduce the illegal copying of its accounting program.
parts.answer: Any three of: a unique product key or activation code that must be entered during installation; online activation that links the licence to one device, so the same key cannot be used on many computers; a licence agreement that the user must accept before installing; a dongle that must be plugged in for the program to run; digital rights management / encryption that stops the files being copied and used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described methods: product key / activation code; online registration or activation tied to a device; licence agreement; dongle; DRM / copy protection / encryption of files.

subtopic: Ethics and software licensing
stem: A software house in Karachi is developing a delivery-tracking app. Three things happen during the project.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by computer ethics.
parts.answer: A set of principles (moral rules) about what is right and wrong when using computers.
parts.working: 1 mark: moral principles / rules of acceptable behaviour for using computers and software.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For each action below, explain why it is unethical, and state any law or licence it breaks.
(i) Faraz copies large sections of program code he wrote for his previous employer into the new product, without permission.
(ii) The office manager buys one single-user licence for a graphics program and installs it on all 20 office computers.
(iii) A network technician reads customers' private messages stored on the company server because he is curious.
parts.answer:
(i) The code belongs to the previous employer, not Faraz; reusing it without permission breaks the employer's copyright (intellectual property theft / plagiarism).
(ii) A single-user licence allows installation on one computer only; installing it on 20 computers breaks the licence agreement and is software piracy, and the developer loses income.
(iii) He has access to the server only to do his job; reading private messages breaks customers' privacy and trust and misuses his access (it may break data protection law).
parts.working: 2 marks per action: (i) code owned by the previous employer (1); copyright / intellectual property infringed or plagiarism (1). (ii) licence allows one machine only (1); breach of licence / piracy, developer loses money (1). (iii) invasion of privacy / breach of confidentiality (1); misuse of authorised access / may break data protection law (1).

subtopic: Ethics and software licensing
stem: A group of university students in Kuala Lumpur has written a timetable app. They are deciding whether to distribute it as freeware, shareware or free software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The students hope to earn money from the app in future. Explain why distributing it as shareware would help them do this.
parts.answer: Users can try the app free, which attracts many of them; after the trial (or to unlock all features) they must pay for a licence, which brings income to the students.
parts.working: 1 mark: free trial attracts users / lets them see its value. 1 mark: users must pay to continue or to get the full version, giving income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one drawback to the students of releasing the app as free software instead.
parts.answer: The source code must be made available and anyone may copy, change and redistribute it, so a competitor could release their own version (even sell it) and the students would find it hard to earn money from their work.
parts.working: 1 mark: source code available / others may modify and redistribute. 1 mark: so others could copy or compete with it and the students lose control or income.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The students used a code library written by another programmer. Explain what plagiarism is and how they can make sure they do not plagiarise the library.
parts.answer: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own. They should credit (acknowledge) the library's author in the app and documentation and follow the terms of the library's licence.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – using another person's work and claiming it as your own. 1 mark: acknowledge / credit the author and keep to the library's licence terms.

subtopic: Primary, secondary, virtual and cloud storage
stem: A newspaper in Peshawar keeps 15 years of photographs on a single external hard disk drive in its office. The editor is thinking of moving the whole archive to cloud storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to the newspaper of moving its photo archive to cloud storage.
parts.answer:
1. The photos can be reached from any device with an internet connection, so reporters working away from the office can find and use old photos.
2. The cloud provider keeps copies on servers in other places and backs them up, so the archive is safe if the office drive fails or the office suffers fire, theft or flooding.
(Also accept: storage can be increased easily when needed without buying new drives; the provider looks after maintenance and security of the hardware.)
parts.working: 2 marks per benefit (1 for the benefit, 1 for expansion linked to the newspaper), for any two of: access from anywhere / any device; off-site copies and provider backups protect against loss of the single drive; easily scalable capacity; no hardware to buy or maintain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two drawbacks of using cloud storage for the archive.
parts.answer:
1. An internet connection is needed; if it is slow or down, photos cannot be accessed, and uploading 15 years of large image files may take a long time.
2. The photos are held by a third party, so the newspaper depends on the provider's security and reliability; data could be hacked or lost if the provider has an outage or closes.
(Also accept: a monthly or yearly fee must be paid for as long as the service is used.)
parts.working: 2 marks per drawback (1 + 1 expansion), for any two of: needs internet access / limited by bandwidth; security and privacy depend on a third party; provider outage or failure; ongoing subscription cost.
